To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

histone H 3 amino acids Q120, R49, and K122 are required for nucleosomes to be properly reassembled and disassembled, and are required for nucleosomal occupancy by Spt6, Spt2 and Spt16 at genomic locations where high transcription rates occur, but not at locations of low transcription rates.

histone H2A/H2B chaperones Spt2, -6, and -16 require histone H3 residues K122, Q121, and R49 for binding to nucleosomes, and that these residues are required for proper histone H3/H4 dimer formation, nucleosome assembly and disassembly, and transcriptional regulation of highly transcribed genes.
the amino acids K122, Q20, and R49 of histone H are required for Stp2, Spt16 and Spt6 occupancy over highly transcribing regions of the genome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of histone H4 and H3 amino acids in regulating nucleosome occupancy and dynamics, as well as transcriptional regulation.
the role of nucleosomes in regulating access of DNA to transcription factors.
the regulation of chromatin structure and transcription in eukaryotic organisms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the histone chaperones Spt2, 6 and 16 are important factors in transcription and their binding is regulated by specific amino acid residues in histone H3.
histone proteins have a direct role in regulating nucleosome dynamics through interactions with histone chaperones, thereby affecting nucleosome occupancy at specific genomic locations.
these histone amino acids are important for transcriptional regulation and that they are required to regulate the binding of specific histone chaperones and the dynamics of nucleosome remodeling.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the amino acids we have studied here are important for histone protein interactions with other factors, and these interactions regulate nucleosome dynamics and chromatin structure.

histone chaperones are required to maintain the nucleosomal landscape during active transcription, and that specific histone residues are required for proper binding of histone chaperons and subsequent nucleosome dynamics.
nucleosome dynamics, nucleosome occupancy and nucleosome stability are all regulated by the same amino acid in histone H3, K122, and that this regulation is dependent on transcription rate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
nucleosome occupancy and histone chaperones are regulated by specific residues in histone proteins.
the histone residues we identified in H3 and H3.3 are important for nucleosome architecture, nucleosome dynamics, and transcription regulation.
the histone H3 residue K122 plays an important role in nucleosome assembly, disassembly, and transcription regulation.
